Subaru Forester SF (2001, AUS) · Denso 64 KB ECU

Subaru Forester Denso ECU Teardown

Static analysis of the 65,536-byte Denso engine-management image from a 2001 Subaru Forester SF (Australian, EJ202 — 2.0 L SOHC NA). Covers the hardware, processor, memory map, calibration format, a full visual catalogue of every code-referenced table classified by its driving sensor, the factory ignition and fuel maps, and the spark output traced to the coil timer register. All maps are oriented RPM on X, load on Y.

01 · Headline

Fuel and spark, side by side

The two primary maps, oriented RPM (X) × load (Y). Fuel rises down the load axis; ignition advance falls down the load axis and climbs along rpm — physical opposites, which is exactly how the pair should look.

02 · The ECU

Subaru Forester — the hardware

The unit this image was read from: a Denso-built ECU for the Subaru Forester SF, consistent with the naturally-aspirated EJ202 (2.0 L SOHC). Two part numbers are on the label — and they are both part/model numbers, not a per-unit serial.

MarkingAssigned byWhat it is
22611AF000SubaruSubaru's ECU part number (all Subaru ECMs begin 22611…)
112500-0103DensoDenso's hardware/manufacturing number (12 V, DENSO JAPAN)
7gdaq000.aus— (in ROM)calibration ID; .aus = Australian market

Factory ECM pinout & signals

From the service manual — the key that ties the ROM to real hardware. Crucially it shows a MAP (pressure) sensor and no MAF, so the ECU is speed-density (load = manifold pressure). It also confirms the sensor set (ECT, IAT, TPS, O2, knock, VSS) and the output wiring: wasted-spark ignition (coil A = cyl 1&2 on E22-3, coil B = 3&4 on E22-9) and grouped injection (1&2 on E22-7, 3&4 on E22-6), firing order 1-3-2-4. Full transcribed table in the repo (docs/pinout.md).

03 · Processor

A proprietary Denso 8-bit microcontroller

This is a Subaru ECU built by Denso; its MCU is the common Denso 8-bit core, the same family Denso used in TCCS-era engine computers (a Subaru application of that silicon, not a Toyota TCCS unit). Denso masked the CPU (parts like D151801-xxxx); the 64 KB program/calibration lives in this external image. The evidence: big-endian 16-bit vectors at 0xFF40; the call encoding 9D BB <addr16> / 9D FB <addr16>; the documented TCCS opcodes 0x33 (load-immediate, operands swapped), 0x05 (DI), 0x35 (test-bit-branch over low 32 RAM bytes); and a textbook reset at 0xFF00 → 0xF810. There is no vendor datasheet.

04 · Memory map

Address space & calibration format

Tracing pointer loads in the code fixed the split: the heavily-written low addresses are RAM/registers, and the calibration tables the code reads by base address sit from 0x1800 up.

RangeContents
0x0000–~0x17FFRAM, I/O registers, scratch variables (fill 0x8A82 in unused ROM bytes here)
~0x1800–0x36FFCalibration data — maps, curves, axes, constants
0x3700–0xEF77Program code (main loop, ISRs, lookup routines)
0xDCB4Shared 2-D/3-D map interpolation routine
0xDAD2Most-called routine — 1-D curve interpolation
0xF800 / 0xEF68Build stamp / calibration ID strings
0xFF00 / 0xFF40+Reset vector / interrupt vector table

Numeric conventions

  • 16-bit big-endian words throughout.
  • Q12 fixed-point for corrections: 0x1000 = 4096 = 1.000×.
  • Self-describing tables framed by 10 00  N0 00  00 0N (N = entry count).
  • Access idiom: FD B9 <rom_table> loads the base, FD BB <ram_index> the index, then the interpolator is called.
  • Storage vs. display: maps are stored load-major (load = inner/columns, rpm = rows). Every map shown here is transposed to RPM (X) × load (Y).
05 · Ignition — identified

The spark map is 0x210E

The routine at 0xDCB4 is the map interpolator. It is called by exactly the primary rpm×load maps, each set up with FD B9 <map> and the same two index variables — rpm 0x08EE and load 0x0966. Four maps call it:

MapCall siteShape (RPM×load)Role
0x23EC0x7C95rises down load, zero top rowFuel / injection
0x210E0x7401falls down load, rises along rpmIgnition advance
0x1E100x6300sparse (mostly 0)Secondary map (combined w/ 0x1DF4)
0x18D20x50BBsmall, rpm-indexedRPM map → 0x09D4/6 (dwell/idle?)

The evidence that 0x210E is the base ignition map:

  • code One of only four maps reaching the main interpolator 0xDCB4, indexed by the same rpm/load variables as the fuel map.
  • code Its lookup at 0x7401 sits in a routine that immediately pulls correction tables 0x20E0 / 0x20F0 / 0x20F4 / 0x20F6 / 0x20F8 through the 1-D interpolator 0xDAD2 — a dedicated advance-assembly block.
  • shape The surface falls down the load axis and rises along rpm — the classic spark-advance signature, and the exact inverse of the fuel map's load axis.
  • scale Scale confirmed as °BTDC = raw / 128: the base cell 2048 = 16.0° and the Q12 reference 4096 = 32.0° are exact round values (128 counts/°), and the decoded surface is physically correct (16° idle, ~36° light-load cruise, 0–4° at high load).

Ignition map in degrees

Applying °BTDC = raw/128 to 0x210E, with RPM on X and load on Y:

A note on the axes

The breakpoint arrays are not stored as plain tables: the rpm (0x08EE) and load (0x0966) indices are computed by near-linear scaling of the sensors, so the axes are close to uniform. The map preamble carries a shared axis descriptor (0800 1800 0006, 6000 000C); the 0x6000 rpm full-scale corresponds to ~6144 rpm, matching the ~6250 rev limit. So the RPM axis is shown as a uniform ~0–6150 rpm estimate. The load axis direction is certain (low→high) but the load axis is manifold pressure (kPa) — the factory ECM pinout shows a MAP sensor and no MAF, so this is a speed-density tune; the exact kPa breakpoints are estimated, so confirm against a log before trusting exact cell positions. The cell values (degrees, fuel counts) are exact.

Update: the coil-fire path is now traced — see the next section. The computed advance lands at 0x0ABC, is converted to a timer count, and fires through output-compare register 0x0212 in a crank-angle interrupt.
06 · Ignition output — traced

From computed advance to the coil

The spark path is now traced end-to-end, from the map lookup to the hardware timer register that fires the igniter — the question the first pass left open.

StageWhereWhat happens
Base advance0x210E → 0x7401map lookup via 0xDCB4 (rpm × load)
Corrections0x20E0…0x20F8chained through 1-D interp 0xDAD2
Final advance0x0ABCbase + corrections, summed in RAM (°BTDC = raw/128)
° → ticks0xDDBC / 0xDE00advance × engine period → timer count
Scheduled time0x0A9Cabsolute fire time, gated by state flag 0x1555
Crank ISR0xE1A4 (vec 0xFF40)reads input-capture 0x0242 + timer 0x0040 → period 0x0938
Coil fire0x021216-bit output-compare; bit15 = IGt output level
  • code Final advance is assembled at 0x0ABC = 0x0ABE (base) + 0x0AC0 (corrections), with a companion dwell / coil-charge value at 0x0ABA.
  • code The highest-priority interrupt 0xE1A4 (first vector, 0xFF40) is the crank input-capture ISR: it timestamps crank pulses at 0x0242 and maintains the engine period that becomes rpm.
  • code Spark fires through the 16-bit output-compare register 0x0212 — its top bit (0x8000) drives the output level, set around a degree→tick conversion. The injector channel is the sibling register 0x0222.
Caveat: the register mechanics (bit15 level + compare time, fed by the degree→tick converter) are verified by control-flow tracing. Which physical pin is IGt vs injector is a strong inference from usage, not scope-confirmed — check on a timing light before relying on it for a hardware mod.
07 · Table roles

What drives each table

Every table is loaded with an index variable (FD BB <var>) that names the sensor or state driving it — a firmer basis for a table's role than its shape alone. Grouping all 69 tables by that variable gives coherent subsystems:

Driving inputTablesRole familyConf.
0x08EErpm×load mapsengine RPM (from crank ISR)verified
0x096613engine load = MAP / kPa (speed-density; pinout-confirmed)verified
0x092422coolant temp — warmup/temperature correction familyinferred
0x090E8throttle / acceleration enrichmentinferred
0x08DC3analog sensor via ADC ch 0x00AA (IAT or baro)inferred
0x0B78…3+auxiliary subsystem groups (speed/EGR?)inferred

The input→table grouping is read directly from the code (verified); the physical sensor names for the non-rpm/load variables are inferred from curve shape and correction count. Full per-table detail is in data/table_roles.csv.

09 · Using the data

Porting to an aftermarket ECU

Reflashing the factory Denso ECU isn't practical (no known community flash tool for this early unit), so the realistic path is to replicate this calibration on a standalone ECU (Link, Haltech, MoTeC, Speeduino, …). The full recipe is in docs/aftermarket-porting.md; in short:

  1. Wire it up. Use the pinout above. Crank sensor is VR/reluctor; firing order 1-3-2-4; start with wasted-spark + grouped injection (crank-only, no cam sync needed).
  2. Set speed-density. Load axis is MAP (kPa) — build fuel & ignition on an rpm × kPa grid (resample the factory 19×11/7 onto e.g. 16×16).
  3. Load ignition directly. The factory map is already °BTDC (ignition_degrees.csv) — copy it in, minus a safety margin. Confirm the ÷128 scale on a timing light.
  4. Fuel via VE. The factory map is injection-quantity, not VE; use ve_table_relative.csv as the shape and set the absolute level from your injectors / 1994 cc / target AFR.
  5. Rev limit ~6250 rpm (start lower).
  6. Tune it. First-start, idle, then dyno/road-tune on a wideband with knock monitoring. Everything here is a baseline, not a finished tune.

Confidence. Processor, memory map, numeric format, the interpolation routine and the fuel/ignition identification are supported by both code tracing and surface shape. The load axis is confirmed as MAP/kPa (speed-density) by the factory pinout; the ignition degree-scale still wants a timing-light check; the spark output path is traced to output-compare register 0x0212 (physical pin inferred). Static analysis of one image — verify against a running engine before relying on any value.
